title: A small segmentation network that runs in under half a second on a CPU
paper_title: Segfast: A faster squeezenet based semantic image segmentation technique using depth-wise separable convolutions
date_note: ICVGIP 2018 (11th Indian Conference on Computer Vision, Graphics and Image Processing), Hyderabad, 18-22 Dec 2018; opening day used
venue: 11th Indian Conference on Computer Vision, Graphics and Image Processing (ICVGIP)
authors: A Pal, S Jaiswal, Swarnendu Ghosh, N Das, M Nasipuri
summary: SegFast labels every pixel of a street scene with about 49 times fewer parameters than SegNet, and runs about 5.1 times faster on a plain CPU, with accuracy comparable to SegNet's.

body.p: A self-driving car has to know what every part of its camera image is: road, sky, building, pedestrian. This pixel-by-pixel labelling is called semantic segmentation. The best networks for it usually need expensive graphics cards, which keeps the technology out of cheap cars. We built SegFast, a much smaller network that still labels street scenes well and runs quickly on an ordinary processor.

Most segmentation networks are large. A network is a long chain of small mathematical filters, and each filter has numbers (parameters) that the computer learns during training. More parameters means more memory and more arithmetic for every image. Two older networks make a good yardstick: FCN, with about 134.5 million parameters, and SegNet, with about 29.5 million (Table 5).

Speed matters for safety too. A system that spots a danger but reacts late is not much help. So we wanted a balance: fast and small, without giving up much accuracy. We were thinking in particular of countries like India, where most vehicles are in the low-budget range.

We started from SqueezeNet, a network designed to be small. Its building block is the “fire module”. It first squeezes the data down to fewer channels (a channel is one layer of feature maps, a bit like one colour plane of an image). Then it expands the data again using a mix of tiny 1×1 filters and larger 3×3 filters.

We made that block even smaller. A normal 3×3 filter looks at all the channels at once. A depth-wise separable convolution splits the job in two. First, one flat filter works on each channel on its own. Then a 1×1 filter mixes the channels together. The result is similar, but it needs far fewer numbers. We swapped this into the fire module and called the result a “spark” module.

The second change is on the way back up. A segmentation network shrinks the image to understand it, then has to blow it up again to label each pixel. We built that upsampling part from depth-wise separable transposed convolutions, which is the same trick applied in reverse. The paper notes that this trick had normally been used only for ordinary convolutions.

figure.alt: Diagram of the SegFast encoder-decoder. The input image passes through a strided convolution, pooling and spark modules that shrink it, then through transposed convolutions that grow it back to a segmentation map. Dotted arrows copy features from the left side to the right.
figure.caption: The encoder (top row) shrinks the image with spark modules. The decoder (bottom row) grows it back, and the dotted arrows copy encoder features across and join them to the decoder's features of the same size.

body.p: We trained SegFast, FCN and SegNet on four driving datasets: BDD, CamVid, Synthia and Mapillary (Table 1). All images were resized to 224×224 pixels, and we did no data augmentation. We also trained SegFast-Basic, the same network with ordinary convolutions, to see what the depth-wise trick alone contributes. For timing we deliberately used only a CPU (an Intel Xeon with 16 threads), because the graphics card we had was too powerful to show any significant difference.

SegFast has 603,288 parameters. That is about 223 times fewer than FCN and about 49 times fewer than SegNet. The depth-wise trick alone cuts the parameter count by almost a factor of 5 compared with SegFast-Basic, which has 2,965,976. On one 224×224 image, SegFast needs about 703 MiB of GPU memory, against 1,515 MiB for SegNet and 3,447 MiB for FCN (Table 5).

body.callout: On a CPU, one forward pass takes about 0.39 seconds with SegFast, roughly 5.1 times faster than SegNet (1.977 s) and 8.7 times faster than FCN (3.385 s) (Table 4).

body.p: Accuracy held up. In pixel accuracy, SegFast scored 83.48% on BDD and 93.58% on Synthia, the best of the networks we compared on both. SegNet did slightly better on CamVid (88.70% against 85.08%) and Mapillary (82.46% against 81.63%). SegFast beat FCN on every dataset (Table 2). The mean intersection over union, a stricter measure of how well predicted regions overlap the true ones, tells the same story (Table 3).

figure.alt: A grid of four street scenes, one per row. Columns show the original image, the ground-truth labels, and the outputs of FCN, SegNet and SegFast, drawn as flat colours for road, sky, trees, cars and so on.
figure.caption: Rows are BDD, CamVid, Mapillary and Synthia. From left: photo, true labels, FCN-8s, SegNet, SegFast. SegFast's boundaries are comparable to SegNet's, and in some cases it avoids SegNet's noisy predictions.

body.p: SegFast does not win everywhere. It did worse than SegNet on CamVid, which has only 367 training images, and on Mapillary, which has 66 classes (Table 1). Our reading is that it works best when the number of classes and the amount of training data are well balanced. With so few parameters it has less room to learn. To improve it one would need a deeper or wider network, but that would be less efficient in speed. The speed result also applies to the CPU setting; on the highly parallel hardware of a GPU the difference in time would be negligible.
The aim was not to beat every record. It was to offer a method that can run on cheap hardware and so reach more people. In future we hope the same compression can be applied to deeper networks.
